title: Sindhi devotees of Nanak
hook: many Sindhi families revere Guru Nanak and the Granth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh Dharma in the West, and Western Sikhs who learned the Guru's word as adults. Your line was newcomers welcome. Who was the newest person in your room? Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.

Before breakfast, a grandmother in a Sindhi family's home covers her head and steps into a small room kept a little differently from the rest of the house. The floor is swept twice. A cloth canopy hangs over a low platform, and on it, wrapped in fine cloth, rests a copy of the Guru Granth Sahib. A picture of Guru Nanak hangs nearby. On the same shelf there might be images from a Hindu shrine too. She reads a few lines of the Japji, then goes to make the tea. Nobody in the house wears a turban. Today we meet a devotion to Guru Nanak that has its own shape.
screen: `A SMALL ROOM, SWEPT TWICE.` → `THE GRANTH UNDER A CANOPY.` → `THE JAPJI BEFORE BREAKFAST.`

segments.voice: Today's word is Nanakpanthi: one who walks on Nanak's path. It's a name used for people who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth whether or not they keep the Khalsa's outward form. In some Sindhi Hindu families the devotion runs deep. Tradition in Sindh remembers Guru Nanak's teaching reaching there through traveling teachers, and some Sindhi families came to hold the Granth as sacred and Guru Nanak as their own. Sindhi devotees gather at places called darbars or tikanas, where the Granth is honored and kirtan is sung, often beside images and customs from Hindu worship. A Sindhi family might name a child at the Granth, or read Sukhmani Sahib at a death. The Partition carried Sindhi families far from Sindh, and tradition remembers some carrying the Granth with them. Sikhs see this devotion in different ways. Some welcome it warmly as love for the Guru. Others are concerned about the Granth being placed beside images, since Sikh practice keeps the Guru Granth Sahib apart. Those conversations are real, and sometimes hard, and they belong to the people having them. What sits underneath both is a line Guru Nanak sang, kept in the Sohila on Ang 13. In paraphrase: there is a light in everyone, and that light is the One; by its shining, all are lit. Nanak's word didn't stop at the edge of one community. It traveled to Sindh, into homes that keep it in their own way.
screen: `NANAKPANTHI: ON NANAK'S PATH.` · `SINDHI HOMES AND DARBARS.` · `SIKHS HOLD DIFFERENT VIEWS.` · `ANG 13: ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · then, large: `NANAK FOR MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a devotion unlike yours. Let your breath slow, and call to mind someone who loves something holy in a way you don't: a different ritual, a different order of things, a mix you wouldn't choose. Don't decide whether they're right. Just see the love in it, the swept floor, the covered head, the few lines read before breakfast. Breathe in, and notice that love. Breathe out, and let it be theirs. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Nanakpanthi. One who walks on Nanak's path. A name for people, among them Sindhi families, who revere Guru Nanak and the Granth in their own way. Today's word.

Your line: nanak for many. Today, notice one way a teaching you value has traveled into a life very different from yours, and leave it room to look different there. Day one thousand three hundred seventeen.
